citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the finite dominated model setup of
[[def-marginal-likelihood-and-bayes-factor]]. Fix a data value $y$ such that
$0<m_i(y)<\infty$ for every $i\in I$. A version of the posterior model
probabilities at this fiber is
$$\Pr(M=i\mid y)=\frac{w_i m_i(y)}{\sum_{\ell\in I}w_\ell m_\ell(y)}.$$
For any two models $i,j\in I$, the posterior odds satisfy
$$\frac{\Pr(M=j\mid y)}{\Pr(M=i\mid y)}=\frac{w_j}{w_i}\,BF_{ji}(y).$$
The displayed version uses the specified jointly measurable density
representatives; no quotient is formed if an evidence is zero or infinite.

Let $I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $N\ge2$ be a finite model index set. For each
$i\in I$, let $(\Theta_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be a measurable parameter space, let
$\Pi_i$ be a probability measure ([[def-probability-measure]]) on it, and let
$Q_i$ be a sampling kernel for a statistical experiment
([[def-statistical-experiment]]) on one common data space
$(\mathcal Y,\mathcal A)$. Assume the experiments are dominated
([[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]) by the same supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$. Fix a specified likelihood density
([[def-likelihood-density]])
$f_i:\Theta_i\times\mathcal Y\to[0,\infty]$ such that
$$Q_i(\theta,B)=\int_B f_i(\theta,y)\,\mu(dy)\qquad(B\in\mathcal A).$$
Require that each $f_i$ is jointly measurable in parameter and data; separate
likelihood versions do not imply this joint measurability. Assign prior model
weights $w_i>0$ with $\sum_iw_i=1$. The **marginal likelihood**, or **model
evidence**, at $y$ is the possibly extended value
$$m_i(y):=\int_{\Theta_i} f_i(\theta,y)\,\Pi_i(d\theta)\in[0,\infty].$$
This is the BCS-02 evidence normalizer
([[def-posterior-evidence-normalizer-and-fiberwise-update]]) specialized to a
proper model prior, and is the prior-predictive density relative to the
specified common data measure. For models $i,j$ whose evidences at $y$ are both finite and positive,
the **Bayes factor for $j$ against $i$** is
$$BF_{ji}(y):=\frac{m_j(y)}{m_i(y)}.$$
The corresponding prior model odds are $w_j/w_i$. No Bayes factor is defined
here using an arbitrarily scaled improper parameter prior.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

derivations.claim: Use the common data space {0,1} with counting measure and the specified jointly measurable Bernoulli densities f_i(theta,0)=1-theta and f_i(theta,1)=theta. By [A1, F3], lambda([0,1])=1, so the uniform prior is proper. Under M_0, m_0(0)=1; under M_1, m_1(0)=integral_0^1(1-theta) d theta=1/2. Both evidences are finite and positive, and [F1] gives Pr(M_0 | y=0)=w_0/(w_0+w_1/2)>0.

By [F3], the degenerate closed interval $[0,0]=\{0\}$ is Lebesgue measurable and has measure zero; [F4] identifies this measure as $\lambda$. Thus the uniform prior assigns the singleton mass $\int_{\{0\}}1\,d\lambda=0$. The separate model atom in step 1.1 instead gives $\theta=0$ prior weight $w_0$ and positive posterior probability.

boundaries.reason: The example supplies two nonempty model spaces and one observed Bernoulli outcome.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 gives model evidences 1 and 1/2, both strictly positive.

Step 1.1 uses finite positive evidence; step 2.1 verifies the parameter endpoint atom is zero under the continuous prior.
Step 1.1 uses only the supplied finite model weights and uniform prior.

boundaries.reason: Example compares positive posterior model mass from an explicit weighted atom with zero singleton mass under one uniform prior; it is a concrete construction rather than a biconditional.
Example calculates m0(0)=1 and m1(0)=1/2 for these two specified models; it does not characterize every prior or observation yielding positive point-null probability.

finite_checks.claim: With w0=w1=1/2, y=0, and evidences 1 and 1/2, the posterior null probability is 2/3.
finite_checks.result: (1/2)/(1/2+(1/2)(1/2))=2/3, while the continuous prior assigns {0} mass zero.
